1) Juvenile dermatomyositis (including amyopathic JDM) — classic heliotrope/violaceous facial rash and Gottron papules in an adolescent with photosensitivity make JDM most likely.
2) Cutaneous/systemic lupus erythematosus — photosensitive malar eruption can mimic the facial findings; would expect other systemic or serologic signs.
3) Lichen planus (cutaneous) — violaceous, flat‑topped papules on extensor surfaces can resemble Gottron papules but less typically photosensitive or facially heliotrope.
4) Chronic actinic dermatitis / polymorphous light eruption — photosensitivity with widespread rash, but morphology and presence of Gottron-like papules make this less likely.
5) Drug-induced photosensitivity or chronic photodermatosis (including porphyria spectrum disorders) — can produce longstanding photosensitive eruptions but less consistent with the specific violaceous facial rash and extensor papules.

Recommended next steps to confirm and stage disease (strongly suggested): formal muscle strength exam, serum muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase), inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), ANA and myositis antibody panel, and dermatology referral for skin biopsy and rheumatology for evaluation and management.
